Path Forward Recommendations to the U.S. Department of Energy: Critical Next Steps for Advancing a Circular Plastics Economy 1. Advance Plastic Sorting Technologies and Establish National Feedstock Standards The success of any recycling or upcycling technology is fundamentally dependent on the quality and consistency of the input feedstock. Current material recovery facilities (MRFs) struggle to deliver sorted plastic streams with the purity and predictability required for chemical recycling. The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) must prioritize the development and deployment of advanced sorting technologies, including machine learning-enabled optical sorters capable of identifying and separating complex, multilayer, and dark plastics. Furthermore, DOE should lead the establishment of national feedstock quality standards to guide MRF operations and align them with the needs of emerging recycling technologies. Without this foundational infrastructure, the scalability and economic viability of chemical recycling will remain severely constrained. Future R&D needs include the development of machine-learning-enabled optical sorting systems, real-time compositional sensing tools, and national feedstock specifications. Commercialization opportunities include deployment of advanced sorting systems and licensing of sensor algorithms. Remaining technical risks include high capital costs, lack of standardized bale specifications, and variability in municipal collection practices. 2. Scale STRAP Technology and Support Sustained Pilot-Plant Operation CUWP has designed and built a 25 kg/hr STRAP pilot system at Michigan Technological University. We have secured DOE funding to complete the design and physically turn on the system. However, we do not have funding to operate the pilot plant, conduct extended campaigns, or perform the critical R&D needed to validate commercial readiness. Future R&D needs include continuous pilot-plant operation, solvent reuse and impurity management studies, and kilogram-scale resin production for industrial validation. Commercialization opportunities include licensing STRAP process packages and co-location at MRFs and brand-owner facilities. Remaining technical risks include lack of long-duration pilot data, solvent degradation, and need for industrial validation. 3. Scale Surfactant Production from Pyrolysis Oils and Expand Application Testing CUWP has demonstrated that surfactants derived from plastic pyrolysis oils can reduce greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 60% compared to conventional petroleum- based surfactants. This represents a transformative opportunity to create high-value products from waste plastics. Future R&D needs include scaling to 1–10 kg/day continuous operation, application testing in detergents and industrial uses, and TEA/LCA benchmarking. Commercialization opportunities include partnerships with consumer-product companies. Remaining technical risks include variability in pyrolysis oil quality, catalyst stability, and limited performance data. 4.
